newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Regulation threatens satellite industry - experts.
newsitem.headline: Regulation threatens satellite industry - experts.

text.p: The burden of government regulation threatens to strangle the rapid growth of the satellite telecommunications industry and should be left to the market, industry experts said on Thursday.
"Regulators should permit access to satellite providers and let the market place decide," said Steven Dorfman, chief executive officer of Hughes Telecommunications and Space Co.
"One competitor is worth a thousand regulators," Dorfman told delegates at the Asia Telecom 97 trade fair in Singapore.
"Governments cannot keep up with the pace of technology, nor can regulators," said Larry Irving, Assistant Secretary for Communications and Information at the US Department of Commerce.
"Governments need to set competition rules not telecommunication rules," Irving said.
Goverments should "get out of the way and keep out of the way" of satellite regulation said Alexander Arena, director-general of telecommunications at the Hong Kong Telecommunications Authority.

Governments also faced the dual burden of being unable to keep pace with the speed of technological advance and the question of how to deal on a national level with an industry that is global in nature, speakers said.
"How can national bodies regulate truly global systems?" asked Bruno Lasserre, International Telecommunications Counsellor at France's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
But the booming industry did need a regulator to ensure fair competition between players, said Olof Lundberg, chairman of Britain's ICO Global Communications Ltd.

"There's a need for some regulating hand," Lundberg said. Self-regulation for satellite operators became an issue in the 1960s and 1970s after regulators sought to limit the number of satellites any country could have to ensure that all could could have the chance to own them.
Advocating "open skies and free markets", Dorfman said he applauded the World Trade Organisation's efforts to ensure "transparent, non-discriminatory, fair access to satellites for operators".

But it was up to the industry to educate governments on the importance of the freer access and provision of advanced satellite technology which "strengthens economies, provides education and provides utilities for businesses", Dorfman said.

Five years of negotiations between the United States and the European Union had now delivered the basis of a new deregulated framework, said Michael Kenney, vice president and director, of satellite regulatory relations at Motorola Inc.
But given the rapid advances in satellite applications, there was concern that the process was too slow, he said.
"Are we dregulating fast enough as a community in partnership with governments and regulators?," he asked.
"We can't continue to go at the pace we're going at if we're going to allow users access to the kind of services they want," Kennedy said.
